extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in fashion, corporate ethics, and media coverage of brand controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A short news/explainer article about instances where fashion brands released culturally insensitive or racist products, the corporate responses, and the broader diversity-related causes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify decision-making power
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental restructuring of who holds decision-making power to prevent future disasters; apologies and diversity appointments address symptoms rather than causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article concludes that preventing racist design failures requires changing who has decision-making authority — e.g., 'someone inherently part of the creative team to call out their crap... a person of colour... black folk in large decision-making positions.' Appointments or apologies alone are insufficient without real power redistribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire and promote more Black employees / increase diversity throughout organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Brands should increase hiring and promotion of Black people and underrepresented staff so incidents are called out internally and avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited opinions and brand statements (Gucci: 'fully committed to increasing diversity throughout our organisation') emphasize that hiring more Black people and cultivating an environment where people feel comfortable to speak up will help avoid incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and adequate corporate response and apology
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly and clearly a company responds when an offensive product is exposed (e.g., Gucci took 10 hours to respond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece contrasts response times and content — timely apologies and commitments to change are expected, but the article warns that apologies alone may not fix systemic issues. Speed, acknowledgement, and concrete commitments matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement internal review processes to mitigate culturally insensitive products
rubrics_metrics.description: Put processes in place to reduce the chance that offensive items reach the market (H&M said they 'put a lot of different processes in place to mitigate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes can include heightened review, signoffs, and checks, but the article notes processes without diverse perspectives may still fail. Process improvements should be paired with diverse decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tokenistic diversity in campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity in marketing must be meaningful rather than tokenistic; semi-diverse campaigns with only one dark-skinned model can read as tokenism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georgina Johnson's critique: semi-diverse campaigns 'largely come off as tokenistic,' so evaluation should consider whether representation is genuine and substantive within creative teams and decision-making roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and marketing should not invoke racist tropes or trivialize suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Products and slogans must be evaluated to avoid invoking centuries-old racist imagery or trivializing poverty (examples: 'Coolest Monkey in the Jungle' hoodie; 'Unemployed' T-shirt; 'Nothing to do. Nowhere to go' hoodie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists concrete examples of offensive items to illustrate the kinds of content brands must screen out; reviewers should consider historical context and the potential for imagery or language to perpetuate racism or class trivialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat repeated incidents as systemic issues, not one-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a brand has multiple insensitive products or controversies, the pattern indicates systemic problems rather than isolated mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H&M's history of prior offenses and the editorial view that 'apologies and diversity appointments address symptoms rather than causes' imply evaluators should look for patterns and underlying structural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider financial and reputational consequences of cultural insensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Culturally insensitive products can have measurable financial impacts (H&M reported store closures and $4.3 billion of unsold stock issues) and damage brand loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing incidents should include downstream effects on sales, store operations, and consumer trust; the article notes customers (e.g., 'people of my generation have lost interest in the brand') may disengage after repeated failures.
